title: Interest Targeting vs Broad Targeting
subtitle: When to guide Meta and when to let it search
youtube_title: Interest Targeting vs Broad Targeting in Meta Ads | Meta Ads Course Lesson 8
description: Lesson 8 of the free Meta Ads course. Should you pick interests or go broad? In this lesson: what interest targeting and broad targeting really mean, the pros and cons of each, when to use which, and a simple test you can run to find the winner for your business.

slides.narration: Hi, I'm Khalil Baghirov, and welcome to lesson eight of this free Meta Ads course. In lesson seven we built a simple customer profile. Today we use it to answer a question every beginner asks: should you choose interests, or should you go broad?

slides.text: Targeting is a *hint*, creative is the filter
slides.narration: Here's the core idea. Targeting is a hint, and creative is the filter. Meta's delivery system decides who actually sees your ad. Your targeting gives it a starting point, but your ad itself tells people, and Meta, who it is for.

slides.title: What each option means
items: Interest targeting: you pick topics and behaviors
Broad targeting: only location, age and gender
Both still use your location limits
slides.narration: First, what each option means. Interest targeting: you pick topics and behaviors, like fitness, small business or online shopping, and Meta starts with people connected to them. Broad targeting: you set only location, age and gender, and Meta searches the whole group for the best people. Both still use your location limits, so a shop in Baku can stay in Baku.

slides.title: Interest vs broad targeting
slides.narration: Let's compare them. Interest targeting gives a clear starting point, but it creates a smaller, more expensive pool, and interests can be inaccurate, because a like years ago is not a purchase today. Broad targeting gives a bigger pool, often with cheaper reach, and Meta finds buyers by itself using signals from your Pixel. But it needs a strong creative, because the ad has to call the right people.

slides.title: When interests make sense
slides.narration: So when do interests make sense? With a new account with little data, because Meta has not learned who buys from you yet. With a very niche product, like equipment for dentists, where the buyers are a small group. And with a small budget in a small city, where a little guidance can help the first results come faster.

slides.title: When broad usually wins
slides.narration: And when does broad usually win? When your Pixel already tracks conversions, so Meta has real data about your buyers. When your product fits many people, like food delivery, clothing or beauty services. And when you test many creatives, because different ads will attract different groups inside the broad audience.

slides.title: Run a simple test
items: One interest set, one broad set
Use the same ads and budget
Compare cost per result after a week
slides.narration: The best answer comes from a test. Make two ad sets in the same campaign. One interest set and one broad set, with the same location and age. Use the same ads and budget in both, so only the targeting is different. Then compare cost per result after a week, not after one day, because results jump around at the start.

slides.title: Your homework
items: Write three interests for your profile
Set up one broad ad set
slides.narration: Your homework for today. Write three interests for your profile from lesson seven, the ones your real customers would have. Set up one broad ad set with only location, age and gender. Then plan the one-week test, with the same ads and the same budget, and write down the cost per result for each.

Now you know when to guide Meta and when to let it search. In the next lesson, we will build custom audiences from people who already know you, which are often your best audience. Subscribe so you don't miss it, and I'll see you in lesson nine.
